name: Pattern interrupt + diagnostic opener
say: Hey {their_name} — quick one. When your front desk is already busy helping patients, do incoming calls go to voicemail or keep ringing?
notes: YOUR PRACTICED OPENER. Downward inflection on 'quick one'. Pause 1 full second after. Smile while saying it. Skip their_name if they only said the practice name.

name: Identity reveal when tested
say: This is Seb with DentaVoice. We help practices capture calls when the front desk is busy. I wasn't trying to sell you anything on this call — I was just curious how you handle it when everyone's tied up.
notes: KILL MOMENT #1. Never dodge. Name + company + one sentence + redirect. All one breath.

name: 'Is this a sales call?' honest deflect
say: I'm not trying to sell you anything on this call. I help practices with phone coverage and I just had a quick question about how yours handles busy times.
notes: NEVER say 'no this isn't a sales call'. 'Not on this call' is truthful — you're diagnosing, not closing.

name: 'Are you a patient?' bridge
say: No, not a patient. I work with practices on phone coverage. Quick question — do those voicemails stack up on busy days?
notes: Acknowledge (2-4 words) → Identify → Redirect with question about THEIR workflow.

name: Voicemail drop
say: Hey, Seb here with DentaVoice — calling because I work with Salt Lake practices on missed-call coverage. I'll shoot you a quick text with the 20-second version. Talk soon.
notes: Under 15 seconds. One specific hook. Promise the text so you have a reason to follow up.

name: Hard gatekeeper block recovery
say: Totally fair. It sounds like you get a lot of these. Look, I'm not going to waste your time — can I send a one-page overview to the office email? If it's not relevant, just delete it.
notes: Pause 2 seconds after 'totally fair'. Validate frustration. Ask for lowest possible commitment. Then honor the exit if still no.

name: Transfer request to DM
say: That makes sense. Hey, who usually handles decisions about phone systems or office tools — is that the dentist or is there an office manager?
notes: Casual 'hey'. Asking for DIRECTION, not permission. Offer two options so she picks one.

name: Callback time lock
say: Got it. Would it be unreasonable for me to try back around {specific_pain}? And is there a better number or should I call this line?
notes: 'Unreasonable' invites 'no' = 'no, that's fine'. Fill specific_pain with a concrete time like '3:15' or 'tomorrow at 10'. Always lock the number too.

name: 'Send an email' — get a specific name
say: Happy to. Who should I address it to so it doesn't get lost in the shuffle? I'll follow up in a couple days to make sure it didn't hit spam.
notes: Getting a specific name turns a cold email into a warm one. Plant the follow-up too.

name: 'We have an answering service' probe
say: That's smart. Quick question — when a patient calls wanting to book, can they actually get on the schedule through the service, or do they just leave a message?
notes: 90% = just messages. That's your gap. This play works for both gatekeeper AND DM objection.

name: Warm open — Office Manager
say: Hey {their_name}, this is Seb with DentaVoice. Your team mentioned you handle the front desk systems — appreciate you taking a minute. I work with practices in Salt Lake on phone coverage. Would it be unreasonable if I took two minutes?
notes: 'Would it be unreasonable' is a no-oriented question. Natural 'no' = yes.

name: Warm open — Dentist
say: Dr. {their_name}, this is Seb with DentaVoice. Appreciate you taking a minute — I know you're between patients. I work with practices in Salt Lake on a specific problem around phone coverage. Would it be unreasonable if I took two minutes?
notes: Acknowledge they're clinical first. Respect the time up front.

name: Diagnostic thread opener (universal)
say: How's your front desk team doing with the workload right now — enough bandwidth, or is it a stretch?
notes: For dentist use: 'How's your schedule looking — booked solid, or gaps you can't explain?' Listen for which thread she opens.

name: People thread follow-up
say: That's a lot on one person. When it gets really hectic, what usually gives first — is it the phones?
notes: Staying in HER world (staff) while nudging toward phones. She opened the door. You walk through it gently.

name: Money thread follow-up
say: What are you paying for the answering service, if you don't mind me asking?
notes: If no service, pivot: 'A part-time hire just for phones is easily $20-30K/year. Have you looked at tech solutions?'

name: Chaos thread follow-up — emotional
say: How does it feel when the phone's ringing and you've got a patient right in front of you and you know you can't get to both?
notes: Nobody asks her this. Everyone asks for data. You're asking about HER experience. Let her vent. 3 seconds silence after she stops.

name: Doctor thread follow-up
say: Makes sense. What does Dr. {their_name} usually care about more — keeping costs down, or growth and new patients?
notes: Collaborate, don't fight the doctor-gate. Use her answer to tailor the framing in Play 25.

name: Revenue thread follow-up (dentist)
say: Do you guys invest in marketing — Google Ads, website, mailers — to bring in new patients? And when you're in the operatory, do you have visibility into how those calls are handled up front?
notes: For dentists. Opens the 'paying to make the phone ring, then missing the calls' reframe.

name: The Gap Question
say: And when those voicemails do get returned — does the patient usually pick up, or have some already booked somewhere else by then?
notes: KILL MOMENT #2. ALWAYS ask this before requesting the decision-maker. Plants the doubt that even returned calls are too late.

name: Mirror her last words
say: {mirror_word}?
notes: Upward inflection. Then SILENCE for 3 seconds. Let them elaborate. Use mirror_word = last 1-3 words they said.

name: Venting prospect — label + silence
say: It sounds like you're carrying a lot right now.
notes: Warm, late-night FM DJ tone. After saying this, SHUT UP for 4-6 seconds. Let her keep venting.

name: Pain Math — People/Chaos thread
say: Quick math with what you told me. If calls go to voicemail during busy times, conservatively 30% are new patients. At $800 each, even losing 2-3 per week is $80,000-$100,000 per year. And the hard part is — you never see the ones you lost.
notes: Use HER words. Say 'conservatively'. PAUSE after the number. Let it land.

name: Pain Math — Money thread
say: So you're paying {specific_pain} and patients still have to wait for a callback. During that wait, a new patient worth $800-$1,500 books elsewhere. If even 2-3 per week slip through, that's $80K+ a year walking out the door. You're spending a few thousand and potentially losing 10-20x that.
notes: Fill specific_pain with their actual number like '$350 a month'. Pause after 'walking out the door'.

name: Label + Summary — aim for 'that's right'
say: So let me make sure I'm hearing you right. {specific_pain}
notes: Fill specific_pain with 3-4 sentence summary in HER words: Emotion + Situation + Consequence. Wait for 'that's right' before moving to offer. Do NOT skip this stage.

name: Grand Slam Offer
say: Here's what I'd like to do. I'll set up a fully configured AI receptionist for your practice — free for 14 days. It answers with your practice name, knows your hours, your insurance, and books appointments directly. Only kicks in when your team can't pick up — safety net, not replacement. After two weeks I send you a report: exactly how many calls it caught, how many were new patients, how many booked. If you love it, $297 a month. If not, I unplug it and we shake hands. No contract. Would that be worth trying?
notes: MEMORIZE WORD-FOR-WORD. The offer IS the product. After delivering, SILENCE. Count to 10.

name: 'Not interested' — one re-engage
say: Understood. Is it because phone coverage isn't a concern, or just bad timing?
notes: ONE re-engage max. If she doubles down, honor the exit with Play 30. Dental community is small.

name: 'Patients won't like AI' reframe
say: Fair concern. The patient's alternative isn't your team — it's voicemail. So the choice is: talk to an AI that books their appointment now, or leave a message and hope someone calls back. Patients overwhelmingly prefer getting an answer.
notes: Don't defend the AI. Redefine the comparison: AI vs. voicemail, not AI vs. human.

name: 'We tried this before'
say: What happened?
notes: After she explains: 'That makes sense. That's exactly why the pilot is free. If it's happening again, you tell me and I stop it. Would it be worth seeing how different it is?'

name: 'Too expensive / how much'
say: What do you think a new patient is worth to you in their first year? If the AI catches even one per month that would've gone to voicemail, that's a 3-to-1 return minimum. And during the pilot, it's free — so you'd see exactly what it captures before spending a dollar.
notes: Never defend price. Always reset to value. If asked for the number before diagnostic is done, say '$297/month — but first, one more question about your situation?'

name: 'Need to talk to doctor' — give her the pitch
say: Of course. Should I send you a one-page summary to share, or would a quick 5-minute call with all three of us be easier? And just to frame it — the pilot is free. No financial decision to make. The only question is: do we want to see the data?
notes: Script HER internal conversation. Make it a no-brainer for the doctor: 'free pilot, no decision, just data.'

name: 'Let me think about it'
say: Of course. What questions would help you decide?
notes: Pause 3 seconds first. If she names a question, answer it, then: 'Does that help? Want to give it a try?' If she says 'just need time': 'I'll send a recap email tonight. Can I check in Thursday?'

name: Close: Yes — lock onboarding
say: Great. I'll send you a short onboarding email today — takes about 5 minutes to fill out, then I walk your team through in 15 minutes. What email works best?
notes: Do NOT over-celebrate. Move straight to logistics. Get the email address before hanging up.

name: Emergency recovery — when lost or blank
say: That's a fair point. Help me understand...
notes: YOUR PANIC BUTTON. Works in literally any situation. Pause after 'point'. Then let them fill in.

name: Graceful exit with website drop
say: Totally fair. If phone coverage ever becomes a concern — dentavoice.co. Have a great day, {their_name}.
notes: KILL MOMENT #3. Get 'dentavoice.co' out in the FIRST BREATH after she says no. If she hangs up fast, she still heard it.
